purpose: Lofexidine is used to help manage the uncomfortable physical symptoms that happen when someone stops using opioids, like heroin or prescription painkillers. It helps ease symptoms like muscle aches, sweating, anxiety, and stomach cramps during withdrawal. It is not an opioid itself, so it won't cause the same type of high or dependence.
how_it_works: When you stop taking opioids, your nervous system goes into overdrive and causes those awful withdrawal symptoms. Lofexidine works by calming down certain nerve signals in your brain that are responsible for those reactions. Think of it like turning down the volume on your body's stress response so the withdrawal process feels more manageable.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects include low blood pressure (which can make you feel dizzy or lightheaded, especially when standing up), slow heart rate, dry mouth, sleepiness, and feeling tired or weak. These are most likely to happen in the first few days of taking it.
warnings: This medication can lower your blood pressure significantly, so you should be careful when standing up quickly to avoid falls. Do not drink alcohol while taking it, as this can make the blood pressure drop even worse. Do not stop taking lofexidine suddenly — your doctor will help you slowly reduce the dose. Tell your doctor if you have heart problems or kidney issues before starting this medication.
typical_dosing: The usual dose is 3 tablets (0.18 mg each, totaling 0.54 mg) taken by mouth 4 times a day during peak withdrawal, which is typically the first 5 to 7 days. Each dose should be taken about 5 to 6 hours apart. Your doctor will slowly lower your dose over time rather than stopping it all at once, usually over 2 to 4 days after the withdrawal period.
